blocks.text: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, PEFT, is a family of fine-tuning methods that freeze the vast majority of a pretrained model weights and train only a small number of newly added parameters, achieving much of the benefit of full fine-tuning at a fraction of the memory and compute cost.

This topic introduces the core idea shared across every PEFT method covered in this module, LoRA, adapters, prefix tuning, prompt tuning, and the rest, before those specific techniques get their own dedicated treatment.
1. The Problem Full Fine-Tuning Creates at Scale

blocks.alt: Full model weights all get updated, requiring high memory

blocks.text: Full fine-tuning, covered in the earlier Types of Fine-Tuning topic, updates every weight in the model, which means storing gradients and optimizer state for the entire parameter count, memory demands that scale directly with model size and quickly become impractical for larger models on typical hardware.
2. What PEFT Actually Changes

blocks.alt: A base model stays frozen while a small trainable addition gets updated

blocks.text: PEFT keeps the original pretrained weights completely frozen, untouched throughout training, and instead introduces a small number of new, trainable parameters, only those new parameters actually change during the fine-tuning process.
3. Freezing the Base Model

blocks.alt: Gradients only get computed for the small added parameters

blocks.text: Because the base model weights are frozen, no gradients need to be computed or stored for them, which is exactly where the memory savings come from, the optimizer only needs to track state for the comparatively tiny set of newly added parameters.

blocks.title: Frozen does not mean unused
blocks.content: The frozen base weights still participate fully in the forward pass, computing predictions, they simply do not receive gradient updates during training.

blocks.text: 4. The Small Trainable Addition

blocks.alt: LoRA, adapters, and prompt tuning are all members of the PEFT family

blocks.text: Different PEFT methods differ in exactly what form this small trainable addition takes, LoRA adds small low rank matrices, adapters insert small additional layers, prompt tuning adds trainable input embeddings, each covered in its own topic within this module.

blocks.text: 5. Why This Works at All

PEFT works because of the transfer learning idea introduced earlier in this course, the pretrained model already carries enormous general capability, and a fine-tuning task usually only needs to redirect that existing capability slightly, a redirection that a small number of well placed added parameters can accomplish effectively.
6. Storage and Deployment Advantages

blocks.alt: A full checkpoint measured in gigabytes is compared against a PEFT checkpoint measured in megabytes

blocks.text: Beyond training efficiency, PEFT checkpoints are dramatically smaller than full model checkpoints, since only the small added parameters need to be saved, the frozen base weights are shared and do not need to be duplicated for every fine-tuned variant.

blocks.text: 7. What You Give Up With PEFT

blocks.alt: Maximum flexibility is traded off against slightly limited capacity

blocks.text: Since only a small number of parameters actually change, PEFT methods have somewhat less raw flexibility to reshape model behavior compared to full fine-tuning, which can update every single weight, though in practice this gap is often small enough not to matter for many tasks.
8. When Full Fine-Tuning Still Wins

blocks.alt: Limited hardware points toward PEFT, otherwise full fine-tuning is still an option

blocks.text: When abundant hardware is available and a task genuinely requires maximum flexibility, extremely different behavior from the base model, for instance, full fine-tuning can still outperform PEFT, though this scenario is less common in practice than it might seem, especially as PEFT methods have matured.
9. PEFT as the Default Starting Point Today

Given how much cheaper and faster PEFT methods are to iterate on, most practical fine-tuning projects today start with a PEFT approach, LoRA in particular, covered in depth in the next module, only reaching for full fine-tuning if PEFT genuinely proves insufficient for the task.
Worked Example
A small team wants to fine-tune a large language model but only has access to a single consumer grade GPU, nowhere near enough memory for full fine-tuning of a model that size.

Using a PEFT method, they freeze the base model and train only a small set of added parameters, fitting comfortably within their available hardware and producing a fine-tuned model that performs nearly as well on their target task as a full fine-tuning run would have, at a fraction of the cost and time.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming PEFT always sacrifices meaningful quality compared to full fine-tuning, when the gap is often small in practice
Choosing full fine-tuning by default without first checking whether a PEFT method would meet the actual requirements
Confusing PEFT with a single specific method, rather than understanding it as a family of related techniques
Underestimating the storage advantage PEFT offers when maintaining many different fine-tuned variants of the same base model

blocks.text: Practice

For a fine-tuning task you have in mind, estimate roughly how much GPU memory full fine-tuning of your chosen base model would require, then consider how a PEFT approach might change that requirement.
Key Takeaway

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning freezes the pretrained base model and trains only a small set of newly added parameters, delivering most of the benefit of full fine-tuning at a fraction of the memory, compute, and storage cost, which is why it has become the practical default starting point for most fine-tuning projects today.
